07 Taxonomy

A taxonomy is a classification tree — technically a graph, and a table still answers it

One parent per node, root down to the lowest category — the products themselves hang below the tree. It is the product hierarchy this section keeps coming back to, and it is the layer where the most avoidable pain lives.

What this section actually decidesNot whether to run a graph engine — nothing on this canvas needs one. It is which encoding you store the tree in, because that choice is what decides whether an agent writes correct SQL over it. Six encodings and where we land come next.

TaxonomyClassifies · one parent per node OntologyConstrains meaning as metadata Knowledge graphHolds row-level relationships

10 Recommendation

Store a closure table for the tree and a segment table for the rules that ignore it

Two questions the customer already asks, written both ways. Switch between them — the recursion on the left changes shape every time, the join on the right does not.

Worked query
Adjacency list · recursive CTE


            

              What happens
              

            

          

          

            
Closure table + segment table

            

            

            

              What happens
              

              

              
            

          

        

        

          

            What the benchmark measured
            
On a controlled seven-question retail-hierarchy benchmark, the closure room answered five of seven with the lowest average SQL complexity of any encoding that answered correctly; the adjacency room answered two of seven and produced no recursive CTE at all. Adding the segment table resolved the cross-branch question every encoding had missed. Small dataset, so read it as query shape rather than throughput.

          

          

            What it costs
            
A closure table stores one row per ancestor–descendant pair, so it grows with depth as well as node count, and it has to be rebuilt or incrementally maintained every time the hierarchy is restructured. Each segment definition needs a named owner. Both are worth pricing explicitly on a deep or frequently reorganised hierarchy.

14 Options

      

        
Four open source Labs projects, each owning a different tier of meaning

        
All four deploy into your own workspace and read the same Unity Catalog assets. None of them is a rival to the others — the question is which tier your programme is actually short of.

        

          

            Tier and project
            Fits when
            Fails when
            The tradeoff
          


          

            

              Tier 1 · Describe what you already have
              dbxmetagen
              GenAI-assisted metadata toolkit with an ontology layer. Classifies tables and columns into a configurable entity taxonomy and emits UC tags, metric views or a knowledge graph.
              Not sized in source
            

            Nobody has written down what the assets mean yet, and hand-curation would stall the programme before it starts.
            You need formal semantics. A taxonomy of entity types is not an ontology and will not infer anything.
            AI-proposed classifications need a human to validate them before anything downstream is allowed to trust them.
          


          

            

              Tier 2 · Answer in place, store nothing
              Ontop VKG
              Virtual Knowledge Graph forked to run as a Databricks App. SPARQL translates at runtime into SQL over UC tables through R2RML mappings, with JDBC federation to sources outside the lakehouse.
              Not sized in source
            

            The data cannot be copied, or it genuinely lives across several systems and you need one SPARQL surface over all of it.
            The questions are traversal-heavy. Every hop becomes runtime SQL and the whole cost lands on whoever asked.
            Nothing materialized means nothing to refresh — and nothing precomputed to lean on when a query gets expensive.
          


          

            

              Tier 3 · Materialize and reason
              OntoBricks
              OWL ontology design, R2RML mapping to UC tables, triples materialized to a Delta triple store plus Lakebase, OWL 2 RL / SWRL / SHACL reasoning, generated GraphQL API, ontology tools exposed over MCP.
              Low–Medium · days to a working graph, 1–2 weeks to a curated ontology
            

            The client wants formal semantics — inferred classes, rules, validation — or you want to pressure-test in days whether they need one at all.
            The real problem is organizational rather than logical. No amount of OWL settles a vocabulary nobody owns.
            A materialized triple store is another copy of the truth, on a refresh schedule someone has to own.
          


          

            

              Tier 4 · Govern what the meaning is
              Ontos
              Data products and contracts on ODCS/ODPS, a semantic-model layer binding UC assets to business concepts, domains and stewardship, a declarative compliance DSL, review workflows with audit trails, MCP.
              Medium · 2–4 weeks for the first domains
            

            The vocabulary itself is contested, and the programme needs named owners, contracts and review to survive its own pilot.
            You need inference. Ontos governs what a term means; it does not derive new facts from it.
            Organizational adoption is the work here, not the software. The app installs in an afternoon; the agreement does not.
          

        

        
Reading this slideThe source treats tiers 3 and 4 as primary and pairs them rather than choosing between them — both sit alongside a Genie stack over the same assets. Tiers 1 and 2 carry no effort figure in it, so we would size those with you.

16 Client need

      

        
“We need an agent that connects what it has read and stops asserting what expired”

        
Four documents are already indexed, and every fact needed below is somewhere in them. Two questions, both answered wrong, and for the same underlying reason.

        

          The indexed corpus
          
          
          
          
        

        

        

          

            

              Failure one · the answer is split across documents
              Wrong company
            

            
“Who leads the parent company of Beta Logistics?”

            

              A · not retrieved
              B · top match
              C · not retrieved
            

            

              What the agent says
              
“Beta Logistics is led by Priya Raman, its Chief Operating Officer.”

            

            
The question looks most like document B, so B is what came back. Nothing in the retrieved text mentioned a parent, so the agent confidently answered the question it could see instead of the one it was asked.

          

          

            

              Failure two · two facts contradict and both look valid
              Retired executive
            

            
“Who leads Acme Holdings?”

            

              D · top match
              C · ranked below it
              Both passages are true statements about Acme
            

            

              What the agent says
              
“Acme Holdings is led by Chief Executive Ray Duval.”

            

            
Document D said so, and it said so in wording closer to the question than C used. Nothing in the index records that the 2019 appointment replaced the 2018 one, so there was nothing for the agent to prefer C on.

          

        

        
One need, not two: in both lanes the agent holds every fact it needs and none of the relationships between them — that Beta sits under Acme, and that one leadership record supersedes another. This is the need behind almost every graph conversation, and it is a memory problem rather than a search problem.

17 Why graphs

      

        
Store the edges between those facts and both questions answer themselves

        
A graph adds two things a vector index has no way to hold: a typed edge saying which fact relates to which, and a supersedes edge saying which fact replaced which. Move the clock and watch the second one work.

        

          

            

              Asked “who leads Acme Holdings?” as of
              
              
            

            

            

              What the agent may assert
              

            

          

          

            Four checks the graph runs before anything is exposed
            

              Lifecycle
              Is this still live, or has a supersedes edge retired it? A correction updates memory here instead of appending a second, contradictory fact beside the first.
            

            

              Scope
              Was it recorded for the context being asked about, or borrowed from a different engagement, region, or client?
            

            

              Authorization
              May this particular asker see it? The check reads the same Unity Catalog permissions as every other asset.
            

            

              Source grounding
              Does a citable source actually state it? Vector search is treated as a candidate generator, never as the authority.
            

          

        

        

          Both failures from the previous slide, with the edges in place
          

            

              “Who leads the parent company of Beta Logistics?”
              Beta Logistics —PARENT→ Acme Holdings —LED_BY→ Maya Okonjo
              The two documents never had to be matched to each other. The edge between them was extracted once, at write time.
            

            

              “Who leads Acme Holdings?”
              Ray Duval —SUPERSEDED_BY→ Maya Okonjo
              The 2018 record is not deleted and not repeated. It is retired, still auditable, and still the right answer to a question asked about 2018.

18 Problem space

      

        
Two independent decisions sit inside every graph retrieval, and they fail in different ways

        
One picture, two controls. A user asks for “everything connected to Delta Holdings” — three entities match that string, and the answer is however far out you choose to walk. Move either control and the frontier changes for a completely different reason.

        

          

            Problem 1
            Which node do we start from?
            

              
              
              
              
            

          

          

            Problem 2
            How far out do we walk?
            

              
              
              
              
            

          

        

        

          

        

        

          

            Get problem 1 wrong and the answer is wrong at every depth
            Resolve to the wrong company and every hop after it is confidently, silently wrong. No amount of tuning the traversal recovers from it, and nothing in the output looks broken.
          

          

            Get problem 2 wrong and the answer is right but unaffordable
            Walk to three hops here and a shared registered-agent address enters the frontier, dragging everything attached to it in. The answer is still correct. The bill and the latency are not.
          

        

        
Why this slide existsAlmost every “we need a graph database” conversation is really one of these two problems, and the two have completely different option sets. The next two slides take them one at a time, in this order.

19 Options

      

        
Four resolvers, and the deterministic one stays the default because the index is the bottleneck

        
Same input every time — a typed string that matches three entities. Read down a column for one resolver, or across a row to compare them all on one criterion.

        

          

            Option
            
Deterministic SQLnormalized name + edit distance

            
Vector similarityembedding nearest neighbors

            
LLM-assistedreads candidates in context

            
User in the loopranked candidates, person picks

          

          

            Resolves to
            Both written forms of the intended company. One entity, two surface strings.
            All three, including a different company whose name sits close in embedding space.
            The two forms of the intended company, with the third rejected and the reason recorded.
            Whichever candidate the person meant. Ranked list in, one seed out.
          

          

            Cost and latency
            Milliseconds. Pure SQL over an indexed name column, with no index to build or refresh.
            The query is fast; the index is the cost. Embedding tens of millions of names is a multi-day build and a standing refresh job.
            A model call per question. Hundreds of milliseconds upward, and cost tracks query volume.
            Nothing to compute, but it spends a human turn before the traversal starts.
          

          

            Precision
            High on spelling and formatting variants, and every match is explainable to a reviewer.
            Recall improves on aliases that share no characters. Precision drops, because close in embedding space is not the same legal entity.
            Strongest on genuinely ambiguous names, because it can read the surrounding context.
            Highest available, because the person asking knows which entity they meant.
          

          

            Fails when
            A real alias shares no characters with the registered name, and the miss is silent.
            It resolves confidently to the wrong entity, and every hop after that is wrong with it.
            The same question resolves differently across runs, so answers are hard to reproduce or cache.
            There is nobody to ask. Scheduled jobs and autonomous agents cannot answer the prompt.
          

        

        
What holds at scaleThe embedding step, not the graph, is the bottleneck — so deterministic SQL stays the default and vector similarity is demoted to an optional edge builder at the fuzzy margins. The two on the right are worth reaching for on the ambiguous tail, not on the whole corpus.

21 Recommendation

      

        
Start with materialized hops in Genie; an engine needs a failing benchmark query to justify it

        
One default, one condition that earns a climb, and one line not worth crossing without evidence. Most retrieval asks are answered in the first lane, on the deterministic seed from the slide before it.

        

          

            

              Start here
              Low · days to two weeks
            

            
Hop tables and recursive CTEs over one edge table, served through Genie

            
Genie writes recursive queries against the edge table directly, and pre-generated closures make the cost of the questions you ask most often quotable in advance. Most traversal asks never leave this lane.

          

          

            

              Climb when
              Medium · two to four weeks
            

            
Your benchmark questions are structured, graph-shaped, and have to be deterministic

            
Compile Text → SPARQL → SQL over the same edges for roughly one-second answers a reviewer can read, and route the open-ended questions to the agentic path instead. This is still not an engine — the SPARQL compiles down to SQL.

          

          

            

              Only past this line
              Medium–high · four to eight weeks
            

            
A graph engine or a partner database, once a benchmark query has actually failed

            
A demonstrated failure, plus one of three conditions: graph applications already in production, deep Cypher or SPARQL expertise on staff, or a real sub-second traversal requirement at high concurrency. Delta stays the system of record and the edges sync outward.

          

        

        

          

            Model serving endpoints have no Spark
            Any engine served from an endpoint needs an in-memory execution path of its own, and anything heavy is precomputed in batch to Delta and served as a cheap lookup.
          

          

            The seed and the depth are separate budgets
            The resolver decides whether the answer is right. The depth decides what it costs. Damp the supernodes explicitly, or one shared registered-agent address prices every traversal on the platform.
          

        

      

      
Databricks × Graph SME21 / 30

    


    
    

      
22 Options

      

        
Four ways to give an agent memory, and only the top rung can retire a fact

        
Retrieval decides what is found. Only the last rung decides what may be said. Most clients are on rung two today, which is exactly where the two failures we opened with come from.

        

          

            

              Extension · not from the source
              Framework session memory
              No build · nothing durable
            

            The agent framework’s own scratchpad or rolling summary. Whatever was said earlier in this conversation is in context, and nothing is written down anywhere.
            A prototype, or a single-session assistant where no claim outlives the conversation.
            Nothing survives the session, nothing is governed, and supersession is not even expressible — there is no store in which one fact could replace another.
          


          

            

              Where most clients are today
              Plain vector RAG, no graph
              Already in place
            

            Embed the corpus, retrieve the nearest chunks, answer from them. This is the stack that produced both wrong answers three slides ago.
            Single-document factual lookup, where the answer sits inside one passage and nothing contradicts it.
            Measured at 0.13 mean judged against 0.51 for a typed graph on multi-hop ownership questions — a roughly fourfold gap. And a vector index has no way to state that one fact supersedes another: the 2018 and 2019 records are simply two similar passages, so whichever matches the wording better wins.
          


          

            

              Fixes connecting the dots
              Structure-enriched retrieval
              Medium · 2–4 weeks
            

            Extract a typed graph from the corpus with schema-constrained extraction, then embed retrieval units that carry the verbatim text and its relationship skeleton. One vector lookup, no traversal at query time, no graph database.
            Enumeration and cross-document composition — the two shapes plain vector search reliably misses.
            It maximizes what is found and says nothing about what may be said. A retired fact that is well connected is retrieved just as happily as a current one.
          


          

            

              Fixes what may be asserted
              Governed graph memory
              Medium–high · 4+ weeks
            

            A typed graph and compiler layer decides what the agent may treat as true, running the four checks from slide 17 at retrieval time. Supersedes edges mean memory updates rather than only appends — the agent can change its mind.
            The agent’s assertions carry consequences, and someone has to be able to audit why it said what it said.
            The longest build in this section, and the evidence is one composed benchmark rather than a track record. Standing it up before rung three answers the wrong question first.
          

        

        
Reading this slideRungs three and four are layers rather than alternatives — the source pairs them deliberately and has benchmarked them as one stack. So the sequence is rung three to fix what is found, then rung four when what the agent is permitted to say starts to matter. The dashed rung is ours, included because it is where a surprising number of agents actually are.

“We need to know who matters, who clusters, and how one entity reaches another”

        
One network, read four ways. Almost every algorithm request a client brings is one of these four families.

        

          
          
          
          
        

        

        
All four families are engine-agnostic — nothing above depends on how the computation is run, or on a graph database being involved. What the choice of engine actually changes is the next slide.

      

      
Databricks × Graph SME23 / 30

    


    
    

      
24 Options

      

        
Three engines run those same four families, and the edge count picks which one

        
None of these is a graph database, and all three read the same gold_triplets edge table and write results back to Delta. The only question is where the computation lands.

        

          Where each engine runs, by edge count
          

        

        

          

            
NetworkXserverless notebook

            Load edges into NetworkX, run PageRank, Louvain or betweenness, write results back to Delta. No cluster libraries, no GPU, no ceremony.
            

              
FitsUp to the low millions of edges, when the client wants an answer this week rather than a platform.

              
FailsPast a few million edges it exhausts one machine, and there is no distributed path to grow into.

              
TradeoffThe least setup of the three, and the least headroom. Outgrowing it means rewriting.

            

            Low · days
          


          

            
SparkGraphserverless Spark

            A GraphFrames-style API built for serverless that tiers its own execution — pure-Python driver path when the graph fits in driver memory, coarsen-then-solve for mid-size, fully distributed beyond that. pip install, point it at nodes and edges.
            

              
FitsThe final graph size is not settled, or one codebase has to hold up at both ends of the range.

              
FailsA hard latency target on a very large batch job. The distributed tier buys scale, not speed.

              
TradeoffOne more package to standardize on, against never rewriting when the graph outgrows its tier.

            

            Low–Medium · 1–2 weeks
          


          

            
NVIDIA cuGraphGPU cluster

            RAPIDS cuGraph on a GPU cluster. Load edges from Delta, run, write results back to Delta for Genie and agents to read. Field-proven on a utility power network — shortest path and Louvain.
            

              
FitsVery large graphs, or batch analytics with a latency target — Louvain over tens of millions of edges.

              
FailsThe graph is small, or nobody wants to operate a GPU cluster for a job that runs weekly.

              
TradeoffOrder-of-magnitude speedups over CPU, paid in GPU time and a second runtime to maintain.

            

            Medium · 1–2 weeks
          

        

        
Reading this slideNo column wins outright — the bands overlap on purpose. But one property is worth naming: because SparkGraph’s driver path is pure Python, the same package runs inside a model serving endpoint, where Spark does not exist. That is what lets an agent compute PageRank mid-conversation rather than read a number precomputed last night. At every tier the durable pattern is unchanged: precompute the heavy work to Delta, then serve cheap lookups.

25 Client need

      

        
“Our graph is hundreds of millions of nodes and queries still have to come back fast”

        
Across this rail the algorithms do not change. What changes is which component is still allowed to run when the question arrives.

        

          
          
          
          
          
        

        

          

            What is allowed to run when the question arrives
            
              At query time
              Precomputed in batch to Delta
              schematic, not a measurement
            
          

          

            

            

          

        

        

        

          

            Connectivity is not coordination
            Naive connected components percolates, and a third of the graph can collapse into one component. Require corroboration — two shared signals, or one rare one — then split residual chains with community detection and rank clusters by cohesion.
          

          

            The scoping cut is a parameter, not a rewrite
            Scoping to the region or bloc the questions actually live in is what makes this size tractable, and keeping the cut in configuration means widening it later is a parameter change. Seed resolution stays deterministic at this size, for the reason set out on the traversal slides.

27 Options

      

        
Three ways in, ordered by cost, and the cheapest one involves no GNN at all

        
Both of the source’s solutions here are high complexity, so the order matters more on this need than on any other in the deck. Climb only as far as the decision actually requires.

        

          

            

              Extension · not from the source
              
              Cheapest way to test the hypothesis
            

            

              Feed graph features into the model you already run
              Compute centrality, community id and node embeddings in the batch job you already have, write them to Delta, and add them as columns to the production model. No new training stack, no new serving path.
              

                
FitsA model is already in production and the open question is whether structure adds signal at all.

                
FailsThe decision turns on the shape of a neighborhood rather than a summary of it. One number per node discards exactly what a GNN would use.

                
TradeoffNothing new to operate, and a hard ceiling on how much structure you can express.

              

            

          


          

            

              Pragmatic first move
              
              High · 4–8 weeks
            

            

              Fine-tune a pretrained graph foundation model
              Ingest to Delta, align per-element features in Spark, export training shards, fine-tune a pretrained model on a GPU cluster, benchmark. Or coreset training — the 1 to 10 percent of the data chosen by embedding and clustering. Demonstrated end to end on public DFT data.
              

                
FitsScientific and atomistic work, where a pretrained model already exists for the domain and the physics is shared.

                
FailsNo pretrained model exists for your domain. A business network has no equivalent of an interatomic potential to inherit.

                
TradeoffMost of the accuracy at a fraction of a from-scratch pipeline — and you inherit the pretrained model’s assumptions with it.

              

            

          


          

            

              Only where the graph is the decision
              
              High · 8+ weeks · served from MLflow
            

            

              Build a purpose-made heterogeneous GNN
              Define the heterogeneous schema, build feature extraction from telemetry, train, register in MLflow, serve. Worked example: partition-skew optimization, where schema, runtime telemetry, query history and key distribution across seven node types feed a model that recommends the physical layout, down to which hot keys to salt.
              

                
FitsThe graph is the decision input, and the decision recurs often enough to amortize a trained model.

                
FailsStructure is one feature of a larger decision. Then this is the row above, or the row above that.

                
TradeoffDecisions learned from structure that heuristics miss, against the longest build in this deck and a model someone owns for years.

              

            

          

        

        
Reading this slideThe source names the order plainly — fine-tuning or coreset training are the pragmatic first moves, and a purpose-built heterogeneous GNN earns its complexity only where the graph is the decision input itself. It does not offer a cheaper rung than those two, which is why the top band is marked as our extension. It is frequently enough to answer the question, and it costs a batch job.

28 Operating rule

      

        
Name the need, standardize the edge contract early, and let benchmark queries decide every climb

        

          
✓
Name the need, lay out the options, then recommendSort the need into taxonomy, ontology, or knowledge graph first — the layer determines the tool, not the other way round.

          
✓
Evaluate the managed semantic stack firstGenie Ontology, UC Glossary, Metric Views, and Relationships before any custom build.

          
✓
Separate metadata questions from row-level onesMeaning over your assets is an ontology question; following one record to a distant one is a knowledge-graph rung.

          
✓
Choose the hierarchy encoding for the readerClosure or materialized path, with named business sets materialized as data rather than prose.

          
✓
Land one edge contractGenie, explorers, algorithms, and agents all consume the same Delta table unchanged.

          
✓
Precompute heavy work, serve lookupsBatch algorithms and hop closures to Delta; nothing global runs at query time.

          
✓
Treat entity resolution as first-classDeciding two records are the same thing is reliably the hardest part of a real knowledge graph.

          
✓
Keep Delta as the system of recordPartner engines and virtualization layers sync outward; governance stays in Unity Catalog.

          
✓
Benchmark before climbingA rung is only exhausted when your own queries fail on it for a concrete, demonstrated reason.

29 Discussion

      

        
Map your needs to a semantic layer and a starting rung

        

          

            
The proposal

            
Write down the questions that must work. Decide for each whether it is a taxonomy, ontology, or knowledge-graph question. Then start at the lowest rung that can answer it, and climb only when it demonstrably falls short.

          

          

            
Which questions must work on day one — rollups, multi-hop traversal, algorithms, or formal reasoning?

            
How are your hierarchies stored today, and which semantic rules do not fit that shape?

            
Has the managed semantic stack been run against those questions, and what happened?

            
Are you asking about the meaning of your assets, or about how individual records connect?

            
Who owns semantic curation, and what latency and concurrency does production need?
